title: decide: should unbounded DELETE/MERGE carry DESTROY_DATA?
description:
OPEN DECISION, flagged by the Effect implementation agent and called out as the weakest
line in the table.

Current state: DELETE / MERGE / UPDATE carry WRITE_DATA but NOT DESTROY_DATA.

The argument for leaving it: what they destroy is a predicate question, not a label
question. `DELETE FROM t WHERE id=3` is narrow and harmless; the label cannot see the
WHERE clause.

The argument against: `DELETE FROM prod.users` with no WHERE is catastrophic, and it
currently flags LESS than an INSERT OVERWRITE. For a security screener that asymmetry
looks wrong -- the unbounded case is the dangerous one and it is the quieter one.

Options:
  (a) leave as-is, document the limitation
  (b) inspect the WHERE clause; DESTROY_DATA only when absent or trivially broad
  (c) always DESTROY_DATA on DELETE, accept over-approximation

My recommendation is (b) if cheap, else (a) with a loud doc note. (c) is too blunt --
it would flag every routine cleanup DELETE and train operators to ignore the flag.

The same question applies to UPDATE and MERGE.
close_reason:
DECIDED 2026-10-02 by Adrian: option (c) -- UPDATE / DELETE / MERGE all carry
DESTROY_DATA unconditionally.

The reason

title: Six mutants in the mutation-survivors CLAIMED ledger have no citing docstring
description:
Six mutants in the CLAIMED ledger are killed by no test docstring.

`verify_survivor_claims.py` asserts these mutants are killed by a named test class, but
no docstring in tests/ names them:

- `x_statement_label__mutmut_5` and `mutmut_8` (class TestStatementLabelOnNonContextClasses;
  only `mutmut_4` is named)
- `xǁ_WriteFinderǁ_recover_target__mutmut_5`, `6`, `16`, `18` are named at a class
  boundary, but `16`/`18` are also named as `mutmut_16/18`; `5`/`6` are named only as
  `_recover_target__mutmut_5/6` in the boundary file

The ledger and the docstrings disagree about which tests claim which mutants. The
convention the ledger is built on is "each docstring names the mutant it kills", so a
ledger entry with no corresponding citation means the kill is real but undocumented.

Pre-existing, not introduced by the mutation-survivors work.

Fix: either cite the six mutants in their test docstrings, or drop the entries from
CLAIMED. Do not leave a kill claimed in one place and undocumented in another.
close_reason: Fixed in ss-mutation-survivors: both missing citations added (x__eval_write__mutmut_26, x__child_rule_contexts__mutmut_3), plus explicit statement_label 5/8 citations. Added scripts/check_citations.py which walks the ledger and reports any uncited claim; it found exactly these two and now reports 0 problems. Note: two earlier regex-based attempts at this audit miscounted (reported 6 when only 2 were uncited) -- the committed checker parses the AST instead.

title: Verify spec.py comment claiming dollar-quoted strings in the 4.x surface
description:
## Problem

src/sparkscreen/grammar/spec.py:88-94 describes the spark-4.0 pin as having the
"largest surface: dollar-quoted strings, STRUCT<..> type-level counting, single-char pipe
operators, CALL, BEGIN...END scripts, 24 embedded Java constructs."

Dollar quoting is questionable. The lexer DOES define BEGIN_DOLLAR_QUOTED_STRING /
END_DOLLAR_QUOTED_STRING, but:

- SELECT $$abc$$            -> REJECTED by the shipped parser
- SELECT $tag$abc$tag$       -> REJECTED
- SELECT CAST(x AS TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE) -> PARSED (4.2 type feature)

Upstream v3.5.1 and v4.0.0 lexers contain zero DOLLAR tokens; only the post-4.2 pin has
them. So the syntax is newer than 4.0 by some margin, and reachable only from script /
EXECUTE IMMEDIATE contexts rather than from a plain SELECT.

## Work

Confirm against a live 4.2 engine whether dollar-quoted strings are usable in any
statement sparkscreen would see. If they are not reachable as claimed, fix the comment.
Depends on sparkscreen-bp4 (needs a real 4.x engine).

## Why it matters

A comment asserting a capability the parser does not have is the same shape as the
Reason.PYTHON_DANGEROUS_CALL invariant: a capability claim that reads as current.
close_reason: Done in 3932122: F20. Claim was false for every line except 4.2 (lexer DOLLAR count: 3.5.1=0, 4.1=0, 4.2=7), and upstream 4.2's codeLiteral is unreachable from statement (absent from all 91 labeled alternatives), so UNKNOWN was already correct on all three grammars. No detection change needed.

title: Add 4.1 and 4.2 differential CI jobs (pinned pyspark, not just grammar)
description:
## Problem

Only live-Spark evidence in CI is pyspark==3.5.1. The differential corpus in
tests/differential/corpus.py encodes one Spark version's behaviour. Every 4.x claim
sparkscreen makes is currently verified against a grammar, not an engine.

AGENTS.md says: verify against a real engine before believing a semantic claim. The
grammar is a good oracle for shape and a poor one for meaning.

## Work

1. Matrix the differential job over pyspark 3.5.1 / 4.1.x / 4.2.x (JDK 17 already wired).
2. Record per-version expectations where behaviour differs. Initial known divergences
   (grammar-level, verified against real 4.1.3 and 4.2.0 parsers built from upstream tags):
   - QUALIFY clause -- 4.2 only
   - CHANGES FROM VERSION <int|str> -- 4.2 only
   - CHANGES FROM SYSTEM_VERSION a TO VERSION b -- 4.2 only
   - JOIN ... APPROX NEAREST BY DISTANCE -- 4.2 only
   - JOIN ... EXACT NEAREST BY SIMILARITY -- 4.2 only
   All six are additive in 4.2, so a shared grammar is sound but imprecise in the
   accept-too-much direction only.
3. Keep 4.1 AND 4.2 as separate jobs even if they are believed not to diverge. The point
   is to be first to know when they do.

## Done already (throwaway, not committed)

Built real 4.1.3 and 4.2.0 Python parsers from the upstream release grammars using
sparkscreen's own port_to_python/generate, redirected to scratch. Confirmed 6 divergences
and 0 under-accepts. Harness is at /opt/data/cache/scratch/grammars/ -- promote to a real
test rather than leaving it in scratch.

## Related

F17, F18. Sequence after the key rename in sparkscreen-hr0 so version-matrix naming
is settled first.
close_reason: Done in 3ce8bd5, merged. Differential job matrixed over pyspark 3.5.1/4.1.3/4.2.0 with fail-fast:false. engine_matrix.py replaces the two-way ternary that mapped 4.1.3 onto the 4.2 grammar. Added a collect-count step because the suite is importorskip-gated and a broken engine would exit 0 having run nothing. 84 passed 6 skipped vs live Spark 4.2.0.

title: split Verdict.UNKNOWN into REVIEW vs UNKNOWN
description:
DEFERRED deliberately (D8) -- this is the last piece, not the first, because it is the
breaking one.

Today REVIEW-for-a-known-DML-statement and we-could-not-parse-it are both Verdict.UNKNOWN.
A dashboard cannot tell an agent misbehaving from the screener failing.
`is_analysis_failure` distinguishes them as a side channel, which is a partial fix.

New shape:
  ALLOW   / DENY   / REVIEW (known effect, wants a human)
                   / UNKNOWN (could not determine -- fail closed)

Re-estimate: closer to 2h than the original 3h. Verdict.UNKNOWN survives as a member, so
assertions using it keep working. The work is model.py + policy.py.

CLI exit codes stay 0/1/2 -- REVIEW and UNKNOWN both map to 2. Same gate, different
queryable reason.

Refs: D8 (sequencing), T3 (the MCP motivation).
close_reason: Implemented: Verdict now has four members; exit codes stay 0/1/2.

comments.author: unknown
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-10-02. Verdict now has four members.

  ALLOW  exit 0   resolved, parsed, nothing objected
  DENY   exit 1   a deny rule matched
  REVIEW exit 2   we analysed it and a person should decide
  UNKNOWN exit 2  we could not analyse it

REVIEW and UNKNOWN share exit 2 on purpose. The exit status is the tool's binary gate
(safe, or a human looks); which of the two it was belongs in the verdict field that
consumers already parse. Making REVIEW exit 3 would break every existing `!= 0` gate
for information they were not using, and the first one to map it to a single error
page would conflate them again.

  delete from t where id=3                     UNKNOWN -> REVIEW
  alter table t set tblproperties(...)         UNKNOWN -> REVIEW
  drop table prod.t (no writable_namespaces)   UNKNOWN -> REVIEW
  CALL p()  on spark-4.0                       UNKNOWN -> REVIEW
  df.write.mode(m).saveAsTable("prod.t")       UNKNOWN -> REVIEW
  spark.sql(f'drop table {unresolved}')        still UNKNOWN
  spark.sql("SELCT 1")                         still UNKNOWN
  oversize code / resource limits              still UNKNOWN

The sharpest case was UNSUPPORTED_STATEMENT: it sat in the analysis-failure reason set,
so every parsed-but-unruled statement was counted as "we could not analyse this". We
had the label and the targets; we only lacked an opinion. That is now REVIEW.

Regression found and fixed on the way: _combine() preferred the UNKNOWN finding as
primary. Once the allowlists began emitting REVIEW it stopped matching, so a plain DENY
became primary and OUTSIDE_ALLOWLIST was dropped from the report entirely. It now
prefers by attention needed rather than by one specific verdict.

UNKNOWN_REASONS renamed ANALYSIS_FAILURE_REASONS and lost UNSUPPORTED_STATEMENT --
the name was lying. is_analysis_failure is now `verdict is UNKNOWN`; the old test
asserting it was computed from the reason independently of the verdict was asserting
the defect, and is replaced by one asserting the two agree.

Recorded as D18 and F13. Ledger is now empty.

title: D17 was an empty heading; the sparkscreen-r50 rationale was orphaned at EOF
description:

Found 2026-10-03 while correcting the roadmap's issue table, which cites D17 for

title: F17: spark-4.0 grammar key is mislabelled; rename and re-map versions
description:
## Problem

spec.py declares spark_versions=("4.0.0","5.0.0") for key spark-4.0, but the pinned
commit 3c28a9c093f1026d76e53d3eb2b846ffb28465c8 is dated 2026-08-03 -- three weeks
AFTER Spark 4.2.0 was released (2026-07-11). It is a post-4.2 master grammar, not 4.0's.

Measured rule inventory (SqlBaseParser.g4):

| upstream   | rules | missing from vendored | extra in vendored |
|------------|-------|----------------------|-------------------|
| v3.5.1     | 184   | 4                    | 121               |
| v4.0.0     | 239   | 5                    | 67                |
| v4.1.3     | 272   | 1                    | 30                |
| v4.2.0     | 283   | 0                    | 18                |

## Verified properties

- Over-accepts vs what the key promises: FOREIGN KEY / PRIMARY KEY constraints, QUALIFY,
  WINDOW all parse; none exist in the 4.0.0 grammar.
- Never under-accepts: 56-statement corpus, real 4.1.3 + real 4.2.0 parsers generated
  from upstream tags. Zero statements accepted by a real grammar and rejected by shipped.

## Work

1. Rename key spark-4.0 to something honest (spark-4.2+ / spark-4x).
2. Decide: pin to real 4.0 (so it rejects 4.1+ syntax), or own it as 4.2+ and map
   4.1/4.2 knowingly. Do not leave the claim and the grammar disagreeing.
3. Add explicit version mappings for 4.1 and 4.2 so --spark-version resolves
   deterministically rather than via prefix fallback.
4. Update spec.py comments (lines ~88-94 claim "dollar-quoted strings" in the surface --
   unverified, dollar quoting is only reachable via script/EXECUTE IMMEDIATE contexts).

## Related

F17/F18/F19 in docs/findings.md. See also the 4.x differential issue.
close_reason: Done in 281a228: spark-4.0 removed; spark-4.2 (32f72996) and spark-4.1 (77bbf77e) pinned to real releases, vendored .g4 byte-identical to upstream, 3806 tests + 4 doc audits pass

title: verify_survivor_claims passes nonexistent mutant names
description:
`verify_survivor_claims.py` reports PASS on mutant names that do not exist.

`_mutant_diff.py` prints `no mutant named X` to stderr and exits non-zero without the
word "KILLED"; the verifier only greps stdout for `"KILLED"` and treats anything that
is not `CONTROL FAILED` as survived. Any `EXPECT_SURVIVE` entry with a typo'd or renamed
mutant name therefore passes forever, silently.

Found 2026-10-03 auditing the mutation-survivors branch.

Fix: check `proc.returncode` and stderr in the verifier, and fail loudly on
"no mutant named". A verifier that cannot fail is worse than no verifier.
close_reason: Fixed in ss-mutation-survivors: verifier now fails on 'no mutant named' in stderr and on unexpected harness returncode. Proven by injecting a bogus EXPECT_SURVIVE entry, which now reports 'unresolvable' and exits 1 instead of silently passing.

- `sparkscreen-znf` (dbutils scope) is recorded as settled by decision in AGENTS.md.
- "2,479 tests passing" is stale; the suite is 2,929.

Fix: reconcile the table against `br list`, close the shipped rows with a pointer to
where the work landed, and refresh the counts. A roadmap that lists shipped work as
open misleads the next agent about what remains.
close_reason: Fixed in sparkscreen: roadmap table now cites D15/D16/D17/D18 instead of listing decided work as open; test counts refreshed to 2,929/17/8 after running the suite.

title: decide: LOAD DATA gets READ_LOCAL_FS on both LOCAL and non-LOCAL forms
description:
Both spellings -- LOAD DATA INPATH and LOAD DATA LOCAL INPATH -- are label `LoadData`,
so the label alone cannot distinguish them. Current table applies READ_LOCAL_FS to both.

This is a deliberate over-approximation and the direction is right for this tool: the
canonical attack is `LOAD DATA LOCAL INPATH '/etc/passwd'`, and erring toward flagging
avoids the fail-open direction.

The clean fix is keying the effect on (label, local) -- reading the parse tree for the
LOCAL qualifier rather than the label alone. Costs a treewalk change; needs a
multiInsertIntoTable or equivalent context to key off.

Verdict needed: keep the over-approximation, or implement (label, local)?
Keeping it is defensible and I lean that way.
close_reason: DECIDED 2026-10-02 by Adrian: keep the over-approximation.\n\n  "yup, let's leave it as is. We're targeting helpfulness t

title: Two mutation-survivors ledger entries point at the wrong test file
description:
Two ledger entries point at a test class that does not exist in that file.

`verify_survivor_claims.py` CLAIMED maps `x__eval_write__mutmut_105` and
`x__default_policy__mutmut_55` to `TestSeverityIsRankedAsDocumented`, but that class
lives in `tests/test_decision_boundaries.py`, not `tests/test_mutation_survivors.py`.
The node id does not collect, so both claimed kills report CONTROL FAILED forever.

Both kills ARE real (verified by hand against the correct file); only the ledger
pointer is wrong. This is the same stale-citation class of bug fixed for
`x__read_only_policy` in commit 8a66fd3.

Fix: point both entries at the correct file, or extend the ledger schema to carry a
per-entry file path.
close_reason: Fixed in ss-mutation-survivors: CLAIMED entries are now 3-tuples carrying the module path per entry; the two TestSeverityIsRankedAsDocumented entries point at test_decision_boundaries.py. Both now report KILLED instead of permanent CONTROL FAILED.

title: Detect DataFrame write sinks (saveAsTable, save, jdbc)
description:
THE LARGEST BLIND SPOT. `df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("prod.t")` currently returns
ALLOW with zero findings, as do `.save()` and `.write.jdbc()`.

Ground truth is already established. tests/differential/probe_dataframe_oracle.py runs a
live Spark 3.5.1 session and confirms all three behaviours:
  - mode('overwrite') on an existing table CLOBBERS it (2 rows before and after)
  - saveAsTable with NO .mode() on an existing table raises TABLE_OR_VIEW_ALREADY_EXISTS
    -- it refuses rather than overwrites
  - an unresolvable table name still MUTATES; the effect is determinate even when the
    target is not

So `overwrites` is a real, observable distinction, not a guess.

Design note: the effect is knowable even when the target is not. `saveAsTable(what)`
carries WRITE_DATA + DESTROY_DATA regardless of how `what` resolves, which is stronger
than the SQL path can promise -- `spark.sql(q)` with unresolvable q is genuinely UNKNOWN.
Encode Effect + optional unknown target, not UNKNOWN.

Refs: D10 (effect axis), D8 (staged sequencing), T2. Oracle probe is committed.
close_reason: DataFrame write detection shipped (22ed358); 51 differential tests green vs live Spark 3.5.1

title: Promote the 4.1-vs-4.2 grammar differential harness out of scratch into a test
description:
## Problem

The three-way grammar differential (real 4.1.3 vs real 4.2.0 vs shipped) was throwaway
code in /opt/data/cache/scratch/grammars/ and will be pruned. It is the only thing that
currently proves the 6 known divergences, and the only guard against the shipped pin
drifting again (F17).

## Work

1. Add a test that builds/loads parsers for two release grammars and asserts the known
   divergence set. Needs java -- so it belongs with the grammar-maintener tests, not the
   ~20s fast suite (which deliberately has no JVM).
2. Consider a test asserting the property that actually matters:
   "the shipped grammar never rejects a statement a real engine accepts."
   That is the fail-closed direction. It held 56/56 today and is the regression guard
   worth having.
3. Enforce that spark_versions in SPECS and the pinned grammar agree -- that is the
   invariant whose absence produced F17.

## Note on how the probe misled twice

First-draft SQL for two of the six features failed on BOTH real grammars, which is the
signal that the SQL was wrong rather than the parsers:
- CHANGES FROM VERSION => 1  is invalid; version is INTEGER_VALUE | stringLit, no arrow.
- JOIN APPROX NEAREST BY DISTANCE needs the APPROX/EXACT prefix.

Worth encoding in the test's construction: derive SQL from the upstream rule bodies, not
from memory of the syntax. A probe reporting a defect where two independent real grammars
agree there is nothing wrong is measuring the probe.

## Related

sparkscreen-bp4, sparkscreen-hr0, F17, F18.
close_reason: Done in 2fad0c3, merged. 26-test pin-identity guard: committed .g4 byte-identical to its release tag, rules and label universe a subset of the release, adjacent lines nest, 4.2-only constructs accepted only by 4.2, and no pinned grammar rejects what another accepts. Has teeth: substituting v4.2.0 under the spark-4.1 key turns it red.

title: F19: record 3.4/3.3 grammar findings -- 3.4 needs a mapping entry, not a grammar
description:
## Finding

Spark 3.5.1's grammar is a strict superset of 3.4's. rules(3.4) - rules(3.5.1) is EMPTY.
3.4 has 172 rules, 3.5.1 has 184, and no 3.4-only rule survives. A 12-statement 3.4-era
corpus (CTAS USING, MERGE, INSERT OVERWRITE, INTERSECT/EXCEPT, CAST to ARRAY<INT>,
ADD COLUMNS, TABLESAMPLE, CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW) parses 12/12 on the shipped
3.5.1 grammar.

=> Supporting 3.4 is one version-mapping entry in SPECS. No vendored grammar, no
   generated parser.

## Why not built now

3.4 is past end of life (2024-10-21). 3.3 ended 2023-12-09. The only managed runtime
still on 3.4 is Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS (Spark 3.4.1), out of support 2026-08-22.

## Decision recorded

Don't build 3.3 or earlier -- correctly absent. Revisit 3.4 as a one-line mapping if a
real user asks. Cost is now a measured number rather than an assumption.

## Note

Popularity data (pyspark PyPI, last 90d, pepy.tech, CI traffic included so stale pins
over-represented): 3.5.x 25.0%, 4.2 16.8%, 3.4 7.8%, 3.3 5.0%, 4.1 4.9%, 4.0 4.1%,
other 36.3%.
close_reason: Done in b21a79f: F19 recorded in docs/findings.md. rules(3.4) - rules(3.5.1) is empty (strict superset) and a 12-statement 3.4-era corpus parses 12/12, so 3.4 is a version-mapping entry not a grammar. Not built: 3.4/3.3 EOL, DBR 13.3 LTS is the last runtime on 3.4.

title: Three false mutant claims in the new test files
description:
Three mutant claims in the new test files are false.

Found 2026-10-03 auditing the mutation-survivors branch:

1. `tests/test_decision_boundaries.py:598` claims `x__parts__mutmut_13/14/15`. All three
   SURVIVE with a passing control. The correct disposition is already recorded in
   `test_mutation_survivors.py` SURVIVORS_NOT_COVERED: `BackQuotedIdentifierContext` is
   emitted by neither pinned grammar (verified by walking every node of
   DROP TABLE `prod`.`users` under both). The two files contradict each other.

2. `tests/test_decision_boundaries.py:508` claims `x_read_only_policy__mutmut_5`. It
   SURVIVES with a passing control, and is genuinely equivalent: `allow.query` is index
   9 of 10 rules, so `break` and `continue` exit the loop at the same point. Zero rules
   stay DENY, not "five" as the docstring claims. `test_mutation_survivors.py:697`
   documents this correctly as equivalent.

3. `x__eval_one__mutmut_21/22/23` is documented as "wording of the unsupported-statement
   note", but 21 is `verdict=None` and 22 is `reason=None` -- the same type-violation as
   the declined evaluate_statement pair, with no wording to pin. They are currently
   unreachable only because that branch is dead: `evaluate_statement` never returns an
   empty list across 45 labels x 3 policy shapes, so `if not findings:` at
   `screen.py:321` is unreachable.

Fix: correct the two docstring citations, reclassify 21/22/23 as unreachable, and note
the dead branch as its own finding.
close_reason: Verified by subagent against the mutants themselves, not the docstrings. _parts 13/14/15 SURVIVE (BackQuotedIdentifierContext emitted by neither grammar; 10 backquoted statements walked under both). read_only_policy__mutmut_5 SURVIVES (allow.query is index 9 of 10, so break/continue exit together; zero rules stay DENY, not five). _eval_one 21/22 are verdict=None/reason=None, not wording, and the if-not-findings arm is dead: 2280 calls over 114 labels x 4 policies x 4 input shapes returned zero empty. All three docstrings corrected.

title: dbutils and dangerous Python call screening
description:
`Reason.PYTHON_DANGEROUS_CALL` is DEFINED BUT NEVER EMITTED. It advertises capability
the tool does not have, which is worse than not having it.

Currently unreached and returning ALLOW with zero findings:
  dbutils.fs.rm("/", recurse=True)
  shutil.rmtree("/data")
  os.system("rm -rf /")

SCOPE QUESTION FIRST, not an implementation question. The target environment is ephemeral
Kubernetes pods, where a stray rm -rf destroys nothing durable. Is screening these worth
it there? The expensive failures in ephemeral pods are wrong writes to a warehouse that
is NOT theirs -- and sparkscreen already covers the SQL path for that.

So this may be deliberately out of scope (see D9) rather than a backlog item. Decide:
build it, or delete the unused Reason and document the omission?

If we build it, the natural home is the same Effect flags: REACHES_EXTERNAL for dbutils
filesystem ops, LOAD_CODE for anything that installs code.
close_reason:
DECIDED 2026-10-02 by Adrian: delete the dead Reason; Python scanning is out of
scope.

  "agreed, let's delete that. s
